title: Heaven
hookLine: less clouds and harps, more being with God and all things made new

cards: Clouds. Harps. Someone in a white robe at a gate, checking names off a list.
The cartoon heaven is so familiar it's hard to see past it. And some of it does come from the Bible: the book of Revelation has harps, and white robes, and gates of pearl.
But when the Bible's last pages describe the end of the story, the center of the picture isn't the furniture. It's a person, and one small word that keeps coming back.

teach.h: THE TABERNACLE OF GOD IS WITH MEN.
teach.b: Here's how Revelation describes the end: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them." With, and with, and with.
Then: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death." And notice which way things move.

Not souls floating up and away, but a holy city coming down, and the one on the throne saying, "Behold, I make all things new." John sees "a new heaven and a new earth": this world healed, not thrown out.
The same small word runs through the rest. On the cross, a dying thief says, "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom."
And he hears: "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise."
Paul, writing from prison, says he'd like "to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better." And to grieving friends in Thessalonica he says, "and so shall we ever be with the Lord."
The churches have their own ways of saying more. Catholics speak of the beatific vision: seeing God face to face. The Orthodox speak of union with God that keeps on deepening, without end.
Protestant hymns sing of home, and rest, and the face of Christ. But in these passages the shorthand is simple: heaven is where God is, and the hope they voice is to be with him.

how: Christians speak of heaven at funerals, in the creeds' "life of the world to come", and in hymns; the Bible's own descriptions come chiefly from Revelation 21–22 and from Jesus's and Paul's promises of being with Christ.

o: a place in the sky where only angels live
the sky above, where the planets move
God dwelling with his people, all made new

games.q: who said it — tap the pairs.
p: to depart, and to be with Christ

s: the Bible never mentions harps in heaven
Revelation has harps, white robes and gates of pearl. but its center is God living with his people.
in Revelation, a holy city comes down
not souls floating away: "behold, I make all things new."
Revelation pictures the old earth simply thrown away
John sees "a new heaven and a new earth": this world healed and made new.

games.q: you're the dying thief on the cross beside Jesus. you have one sentence left. what do you ask?
o: "if thou be Christ, save thyself and us."
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom."
games.why: he asks to be remembered, and hears: "to day shalt thou be with me in paradise." no map of the place. a person, and a promise: with me.

practice: Bring back one moment of real joy: a table full of people you love, a morning by the sea, a child laughing until they can't stop.

Then take away the shadow that often comes with joy, the knowing that it will end: no clock, no goodbyes, nothing lost. If you pray, thank God for that hope; if you don't, just rest in the shape of it.

wordCard.voice: Heaven. In the Bible's last pages, less a place above the clouds than God living with his people, and all things made new.

orig.note: Greek: heaven, and also the sky; one word for both.

carryVoice: Your line: with him. Not the furniture; the company. I'll be here tomorrow.
